english_translation: The wind is blowing strongly from the east.

dialogue.shona: Mhepo iri kuvhuvhuta zvakasimba kubva kumabvazuva.
dialogue.english: The wind is blowing strongly from the east.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Mhepo [wind / fresh air] • iri [iri] • kuvhuvhuta [to / at vhuvhuta] • zvakasimba [zvakasimba] • kubva [to / at bva] • kumabvazuva [to / at mabvazuva]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakasimba')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakasimba' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Pointing Out Things: Demonstratives ('iri' = 'this / that / here')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, words for 'this/these' and 'that/those' (like 'iri') come AFTER the noun they point to and mirror the noun's group! Near demonstratives ('this / these / right here') repeat the noun class vowel: 'mwana uyu' (this child), 'nyama iyi' (this meat), 'kapu iyi' (this cup), 'bhuku iri' (this book), 'zvinhu izvi' (these things). Replacing the final vowel with '-o' shifts the meaning to 'that / those / there': 'uyo' (that person), 'iyo' (that one), 'uko' (over there).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Near Demonstrative ('uyu/iyi/iri/ichi/izvi' = this/these) | replace final vowel with '-o' ('uyo/iyo/iro/icho/izvo' = that/those)

cultural_notes.title: Cardinal Directions in Shona: East ('Mabvazuva') & West ('Madokero')
cultural_notes.content: Notice how poetic Shona cardinal directions are! East is 'mabvazuva'—literally 'where the sun comes from' ('kubva' + 'zuva')—while West is 'madokero' ('where the sun sets'). Prevailing moist winds from the Indian Ocean blow inland from the east ('kubva kumabvazuva').

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Shiri diki dziri kuimba pamusoro pemuti', what are the small birds doing?
options: Singing at the top of the tree
Looking for seeds in the field
active_exercises.correct_answer: Singing at the top of the tree
active_exercises.explanation: 'Shiri diki' = 'small birds', 'dziri kuimba' = 'are singing', 'pamusoro pemuti' = 'at the top of the tree'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new nature sentence into English: 'Makomo makuru anoonekwa kure seri kwerwizi.'
options: Two rhinoceroses are grazing peacefully in the valley.
The farmers planted maize and groundnuts after the rain.
Dark clouds have covered the sky this afternoon.
Large mountains can be seen far away beyond the river.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Large mountains can be seen far away beyond the river.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Makomo makuru' = 'Large mountains', 'anoonekwa' = 'are seen / can be seen', 'kure seri kwerwizi' = 'far away beyond the river'.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Hupfu hwapera mumba', why does 'hwapera' ('has run out') start with 'hwa-'?
options: Because 'hupfu' (maize meal) belongs to the 'hu-' noun group, which uses 'hwa-' in the recent past
Because it refers to a person cooking in the kitchen
active_exercises.correct_answer: Because 'hupfu' (maize meal) belongs to the 'hu-' noun group, which uses 'hwa-' in the recent past
active_exercises.explanation: Nouns starting with 'hu-' (like 'hupfu') use 'hu-' / 'hwa-' subject prefixes on the verb.
